# Lab 4 - Single-cell RNA-seq data wrangling

::: {.callout-note icon='true'}

## Notes

The estimated time for this lab is around 1h20.

:::

::: {.callout-tip icon='true'}

## Aims

- Perform basic quality control on single-cell RNA-seq data
- Filter cells and features in single-cell RNA-seq data
- Compute and store new information in a `SingleCellExperiment` object
- Check housekeeping genes and gene set expression in single-cell RNA-seq data
- Plot embeddings of single-cell RNA-seq data

:::

## Introduction

Data produced in a single cell RNA-seq experiment has several interesting
characteristics that make it distinct from data produced in a bulk population
RNA-seq experiment.

Two characteristics that are important to keep in mind when working with
scRNA-Seq are drop-out (the excessive amount of zeros due to limiting mRNA) and
the potential for quality control (QC) metrics to be confounded with biology.
This combined with the ability to measure heterogeniety from cells in samples
has shifted the field away from the typical analysis in population-based RNA-Seq.

Here we demonstrate some approaches to quality control, followed by identifying
and analyzing cell subsets.

### Load necessary packages

When loading libraries, we are asking R to load code for us written by someone
else. It is a convenient way to leverage and reproduce methodology developed by others.

::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

Following the previous labs, load the necessary libraries for this analysis.

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

```{r filename = "R"}
library(tidyverse)
library(SingleCellExperiment)
```

:::
:::

:::
:::

### Create a `SingleCellExperiment` object from scratch

In the previous lab, we have been working with `airway` object (a
`SummarizedExperiment` object) and `sce`, a `SingleCellExperiment` object.
We will now create a toy `SingleCellExperiment` object from scratch, using the
`SingleCellExperiment` constructor.

To create a `SingleCellExperiment` object, we need to provide the following:

- `colData`: a data frame (or tibble) with columns corresponding to cell metadata.
- `rowData`: a data frame (or tibble) with columns corresponding to gene metadata.
- `assays`: a list of matrices, each matrix corresponding to a different assay. The first matrix is typically the counts matrix.

```{r filename = "R"}
cd <- tibble(idx = paste0('cell', 1:100))  ## `cd` stands for colData
cd

rd <- tibble(
    gene_name = paste0('gene', 1:10),
    gene_type = factor(rep(c('protein_coding', 'non_coding'), each = 5))
) ## `rd` stands for rowData
rd

cnts <- matrix(rpois(1000, 5), ncol = 100) ## `cnts` stands for counts

dim(cd)
dim(rd)
dim(cnts)

nrow(cd) == ncol(cnts)
nrow(rd) == nrow(cnts)

toy_sce <- SingleCellExperiment(
    colData = cd,
    rowData = rd,
    assays = list('counts' = cnts)
)
toy_sce
colData(toy_sce)
rowData(toy_sce)
assays(toy_sce)
assays(toy_sce)[["counts"]][1:10, 1:10]
```

### Read in kidney organoid counts matrix

We will now analyze a real human scRNAseq dataset, generated from iPSC-derived
kidney organoids ([Combes et al., Genome Medicine 2019](https://doi.org/10.1186/s13073-019-0615-0)).
It is freely available from [GEO: link](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE114802).
We start by downloading the cell, features and counts matrix of the fourth organoid (`org4`).

::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

Inspect the GEO page and get the downloadable links for each file

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

The links are listed in the "Supplementary file" box at the bottom of the GEO
page. We use `BiocFileCache` (see [Lab 3](Lab3_Rbioc.qmd)) to download them
once, and get the path of their local copy:

```{r filename = "R"}
library(BiocFileCache)
bfc <- BiocFileCache(ask = FALSE)
url <- 'https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/series/GSE114nnn/GSE114802/suppl/GSE114802_org4_'
barcodes_file <- bfcrpath(bfc, paste0(url, 'barcodes.tsv.gz'))
genes_file <- bfcrpath(bfc, paste0(url, 'genes.tsv.gz'))
counts_file <- bfcrpath(bfc, paste0(url, 'counts.csv.gz'))
```

:::
:::

:::
:::

In this dataset, the barcodes file contains the cell barcodes, the genes file
contains the gene names, and the counts file contains the counts matrix.
We can import the data into R using the `read_tsv()` and `read_csv()` functions
(already available in the loaded `tidyverse` package).

For example, to read the barcodes file, we can use the following command:

```{r filename = "R"}
cells <- read_tsv(barcodes_file, col_names = FALSE)
head(cells)
```

::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

Also read the genes and counts files into R.

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

```{r filename = "R"}
genes <- read_tsv(genes_file, col_names = FALSE)
genes

counts <- read_csv(counts_file, col_names = TRUE)
counts[1:10, 1:6]
```

:::
:::

Note how the first column of the counts dataframe is the gene names. We will
need to strip this column, and turn the data frame into a matrix. Most of the
entries of this matrix are zeros: we store it as a *sparse* matrix (from the
`Matrix` package), which only records the non-zero entries.

```{r filename = "R"}
counts <- as.matrix(counts[, -1])
rownames(counts) <- genes$X1
counts <- as(counts, 'dgCMatrix')
counts[1:10, 1:6]
```

:::
:::

::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

Coerce the data into a `SingleCellExperiment` object.

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

```{r filename = "R"}
sce <- SingleCellExperiment(
    colData = cells,
    rowData = genes,
    assays = list('counts' = counts)
)
sce
```

:::
:::

:::
:::

::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

Examine the `SingleCellExperiment` object you've just created. Get an idea of
the size of the dataset, the different data available, etc.

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

```{r filename = "R"}
colData(sce)
rowData(sce)
metadata(sce)
dim(sce)
assays(sce)
counts(sce)[1:10, 1:10]
reducedDims(sce)
```

:::
:::

:::
:::

## Basic QCs

You can learn a lot about your scRNA-seq data's quality with simple plotting.
Let's do some plotting to look at the number of reads per cell, reads per genes,
expressed genes per cell (often called complexity), and rarity of genes (cells
expressing genes).

::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

Plot the number of counts per cell, the number of expressed genes per cell, and
the relationship between the two.

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

```{r filename = "R"}
counts_per_cell <- Matrix::colSums(counts)
counts_per_gene <- Matrix::rowSums(counts)
genes_per_cell <- Matrix::colSums(counts > 0) # count gene only if it has non-zero reads mapped.
hist(log10(counts_per_cell+1), main = '# of counts per cell', col = 'wheat')
hist(log10(genes_per_cell+1), main = '# of expressed genes per cell', col = 'wheat')
plot(counts_per_cell, genes_per_cell, log = 'xy', col = 'wheat')
title('Counts vs genes per cell')
```

:::
:::

:::
:::

::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

Look at the summary counts for genes and cells. Can you plot a histogram of
counts per gene in log10 scale?

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

```{r filename = "R"}
cells_per_gene <- Matrix::rowSums(counts > 0) # only count cells where the gene is expressed
hist(log10(cells_per_gene+1), main = '# of cells expressing each gene', col = 'wheat')
```

:::
:::

:::
:::

A very useful plot is the distribution of library complexity in the sequencing
run, typically shown as a lineplot of the number of detected UMI per cell, with
cells ranked in decreasing order. One can use such plot to investigate
observations (potential cells) that are actually failed libraries (lower end
outliers) or observations that are cell doublets (higher end outliers).

::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

Plot cells ranked by their number of detected genes. Comment.

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

```{r filename = "R"}
plot(
    sort(genes_per_cell, decreasing = TRUE),
    xlab = 'cell', log = 'y', main = '# of genes per cell (ordered)',
    type = 'l'
)
```

:::
:::

:::
:::

Several QCs can be automatically computed using `quickRnaQc.se()` from the
`scrapper` package. `scrapper` provides fast `C++` implementations of most
steps of a scRNA-seq analysis (QC, normalization, variance modelling, PCA,
clustering, marker detection...).

::: {.callout-note icon='true'}
## `scuttle` and `scran` are being replaced by `scrapper`

In previous `Bioconductor` releases, quality control metrics were computed
with `scuttle::quickPerCellQC()` or `scuttle::addPerCellQCMetrics()`. Since
`Bioconductor 3.24`, these functions (and most of `scuttle` and `scran`) are
deprecated in favour of `scrapper`. You will still find them in many tutorials
and in the [OSCA book](https://bioconductor.org/books/release/OSCA/).
:::

`quickRnaQc.se()` computes, for each cell, the total number of counts (`sum`),
the number of detected genes (`detected`) and the proportion of counts
assigned to any `subsets` of genes (e.g. mitochondrial genes). It then
suggests filtering thresholds (cells with too few counts or detected genes,
or with a too high proportion of mitochondrial counts, compared to the bulk of
cells), and adds a `keep` column to the `colData()`.

```{r filename = "R"}
toy_sce <- scrapper::quickRnaQc.se(toy_sce, subsets = list())
colData(toy_sce)
metadata(toy_sce)$qc$thresholds
table(toy_sce$keep)
```

::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

Run `quickRnaQc.se()` on the `SingleCellExperiment` object, providing the list
of mitochondrial genes as a subset. Inspect the new `colData` of the object.
How many cells would be filtered out? Why?

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

```{r filename = "R"}
mito <- rownames(sce)[grepl("^MT-", rowData(sce)$X2)]
mito
sce <- scrapper::quickRnaQc.se(sce, subsets = list(mito = mito))
colData(sce)
metadata(sce)$qc$thresholds
table(sce$keep)
```

:::
:::

:::
:::

## Access to stored informations

### Assay slots

For typical scRNA-seq experiments, a `SingleCellExperiment` can have multiple
assays, corresponding to different metrics. The most basic one is `counts`.
Different assays store different 'transformations' of the `counts` (e.g. `logcounts`).

For example, one can compute mean-centered counts and store it in a new slot.

```{r filename = "R"}
mean_centered_counts <- scale(counts(toy_sce), center = TRUE, scale = FALSE)
assay(toy_sce, 'mean_centered') <- mean_centered_counts
assays(toy_sce)
assay(toy_sce, 'mean_centered')[1:10, 1:10]
mean(assay(toy_sce, 'mean_centered'))
```

::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

Try to manually compute logcounts from counts and store it in a new slot.

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

```{r filename = "R"}
assay(sce, 'logcounts') <- log10(counts(sce) + 1)
logcounts(sce)[1:10, 1:10]
```

Note that this is a very crude transformation, which does not account for
differences in sequencing depth between cells: we will see in the next lectures
and labs how to properly normalize counts (e.g. with `scrapper::normalizeRnaCounts.se()`).

:::
:::

:::
:::

### Embeddings

Embeddings allow for a representation of large-scale data (N cells x M genes)
into smaller dimensions (e.g. 2-50 dimensions). Typical embeddings can be PCA,
t-SNE, UMAP, etc... Many embeddings can be computed using `run...()` functions
from Bioconductor packages (e.g. `scater`, `scrapper`, ...).

For example, one can compute PCA and store it in a new slot.

```{r filename = "R", warning = FALSE}
library(scater)

logcounts(toy_sce) <- log10(counts(toy_sce) + 1)
toy_sce <- scater::runPCA(toy_sce, ncomponents = 2)
reducedDims(toy_sce)
reducedDim(toy_sce, 'PCA')[1:10, ]
plotReducedDim(toy_sce, 'PCA')
```

::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

Try to compute PCA, t-SNE and UMAP embeddings of the kidney organoid dataset
using `runPCA()`, `runTSNE()` and `runUMAP()` from `scater` package.

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

```{r filename = "R"}
sce <- scater::runPCA(sce)
plotReducedDim(sce, "PCA")

sce <- scater::runTSNE(sce)
plotReducedDim(sce, "TSNE")

sce <- scater::runUMAP(sce)
plotReducedDim(sce, "UMAP", colour_by = 'sum')
plotReducedDim(sce, "UMAP", colour_by = 'detected')
```

:::
:::

:::
:::

## Filtering cells and features

### Pre-filtering

Filtering operations are often performed on the `SingleCellExperiment` object,
for example to remove low-quality cells (columns) or genes (rows).

To do this, one can use standard R syntax to subset the `SingleCellExperiment` object.

```{r filename = "R"}
toy_sce_filtered <- toy_sce[rowData(toy_sce)$gene_type == 'protein_coding', toy_sce$sum > 50]
toy_sce_filtered
```

::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

Filter the SCE to only include cells that have a complexity of 2000 genes or
more and genes that are are expressed in 10 or more cells.

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

```{r filename = "R"}
sce_filtered <- sce[
    Matrix::rowSums(counts(sce) > 0) >= 10,
    Matrix::colSums(counts(sce) > 0) >= 2000
]
sce_filtered
```
:::
:::

:::
:::

Almost all our analysis will be on this single object, of class
`SingleCellExperiment`. This object contains various "slots" that will store not
only the raw count data, but also the results from various computations below.
This has the advantage that we do not need to keep track of inidividual variables
of interest - they can all be collapsed into a single object as long as these
slots are pre-defined.

### Filtering low-quality cells: mitochondrial counts

For each cell, we can calculate the percentage of counts mapping on
mitochondrial genes and store it in a column `percent_mito` in our `colData()`.

```{r filename = "R"}
rowData(sce_filtered)
mito_genes <- rownames(sce_filtered)[grep(pattern = "^MT-", x = rowData(sce_filtered)$X2)]
mito_genes
mito_genes_counts <- counts(sce_filtered)[mito_genes, ]
percent_mito <- Matrix::colSums(mito_genes_counts) / sce_filtered$sum
hist(percent_mito*100, main = '% of total counts over mitochondrial genes', col = 'wheat')
colData(sce_filtered)$percent_mito <- percent_mito
table(colData(sce_filtered)$percent_mito > 0.1)
```

::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

Remove cells with a % of mitochondrial counts greater than 10%.

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

```{r filename = "R"}
sce_filtered <- sce_filtered[
    ,
    sce_filtered$percent_mito <= 0.10
]
sce_filtered
```

:::
:::

:::
:::

### Checking housekeeping genes

Another metric we use is the number of house keeping genes expressed in a cell.
These genes reflect commomn processes active in a cell and hence are a good
global quality measure. They are also abundant and are usually steadliy expressed
in cells, thus less sensitive to the high dropout.

We first load the list of housekeeping genes curated by
[Tirosh et al., Science 2016](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aad0501) (shipped
with this book), match them to the genes in the `rowData` of the
`SingleCellExperiment` object (using `match` and `rownames`), remove `NA`s
(genes not found in the `rowData`), and store the list of housekeeping genes in
a new variable.

```{r filename = "R"}
# Load the list of housekeeping genes
hk_file <- system.file("extdata", "tirosh_house_keeping.txt", package = "scRNAseqPhysalia2026")
hkgenes <- read.table(hk_file, skip = 2)
hkgenes <- as.vector(hkgenes$V1)
hkgenes <- rownames(sce_filtered)[match(hkgenes, rowData(sce_filtered)$X2)]
hkgenes <- hkgenes[!is.na(hkgenes)]
hkgenes
```

::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

Calculate the number of expressed housekeeping genes per cell (genes with a
count > 0) and store the number of expressed housekeeping genes per cell in `colData`.

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

```{r filename = "R"}
colData(sce_filtered)$n_expressed_hkgenes <- Matrix::colSums(counts(sce_filtered)[hkgenes, ] > 0)
table(colData(sce_filtered)$n_expressed_hkgenes)
```

:::
:::

:::
:::

::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

Plot (in a boxplot) the relationship between the # of detected housekeeping
genes and the total UMI count (or # of detected genes) per cell. Comment.

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

```{r filename = "R"}
boxplot(colData(sce_filtered)$sum ~ colData(sce_filtered)$n_expressed_hkgenes)
boxplot(colData(sce_filtered)$detected ~ colData(sce_filtered)$n_expressed_hkgenes)
```

:::
:::

:::
:::

::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

Remove cells with a # of expressed housekeeping genes greater than 85.

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

```{r filename = "R"}
sce_filtered <- sce_filtered[, sce_filtered$n_expressed_hkgenes <= 85]
sce_filtered
```

:::
:::

:::
:::

### Checking gene set expression

Sometimes we want to ask what is the expression of a gene / a set of a genes
across cells. This set of genes may make up a gene expression program we are
interested in. Another benefit at looking at gene sets is it reduces the effects
of drop outs.

Let's look at genes involved in the stress signature upon cell dissociation.
We calculate these genes average expression levels on the single cell level.

```{r filename = "R"}
genes_dissoc <- c("ATF3", "BTG2", "CEBPB", "CEBPD", "CXCL3", "CXCL2", "CXCL1", "DNAJA1", "DNAJB1", "DUSP1", "EGR1", "FOS", "FOSB", "HSP90AA1", "HSP90AB1", "HSPA1A", "HSPA1B", "HSPA1A", "HSPA1B", "HSPA8", "HSPB1", "HSPE1", "HSPH1", "ID3", "IER2", "JUN", "JUNB", "JUND", "MT1X", "NFKBIA", "NR4A1", "PPP1R15A", "SOCS3", "ZFP36")
genes_dissoc <- rownames(sce_filtered)[match(genes_dissoc, rowData(sce_filtered)$X2)]
genes_dissoc <- unique(genes_dissoc[!is.na(genes_dissoc)])
```

::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

Calculate the average gene set expression for each cell.

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

```{r filename = "R"}
ave_expr_genes_dissoc <- Matrix::colMeans(logcounts(sce_filtered[genes_dissoc, ]))
colData(sce_filtered)$ave_expr_genes_dissoc <- ave_expr_genes_dissoc
```

:::
:::

:::
:::

::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

Plot an embedding of the dataset, using a color scale representing the average
expression of genes involved in the stress signature upon cell dissociation. Comment.

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

```{r filename = "R"}
plotReducedDim(sce_filtered, dimred = 'PCA', colour_by = 'ave_expr_genes_dissoc')
plotReducedDim(sce_filtered, dimred = 'UMAP', colour_by = 'ave_expr_genes_dissoc')
```
